title: One-Variable Data: Distributions and Measures
subtitle: Master mean, median, mode, spread, standard deviation, and box plots

sections.title: Measures of Center vs. Measures of Spread
sections.content:
When the SAT gives you a data set, it tests two categories of statistics:

**Measures of center** (where the data is located):
- **Mean** (average): sum ÷ count
- **Median**: middle value when sorted
- **Mode**: most frequent value

**Measures of spread** (how much the data varies):
- **Range**: max − min
- **Interquartile range (IQR)**: Q3 − Q1
- **Standard deviation**: average distance from the mean

**Key insight:** mean is sensitive to outliers; median and IQR are resistant to them.

sections.title: Type 1: Finding the Median
Step-by-Step Median Process
sections.content:
**Step 1:** Sort the data from smallest to largest.
**Step 2:** Count the number of values ($n$).
- If $n$ is **odd**: median = the middle value (position $\frac{n+1}{2}$)
- If $n$ is **even**: median = average of the two middle values (positions $\frac{n}{2}$ and $\frac{n}{2}+1$)

**From a frequency table:** write out all values (including repeats) before finding the position.
**From a bar graph:** the height of each bar tells you how many times to repeat each value.

sections.title: Example: Median from a List
Example: Median from a Frequency Table
sections.problem: Charging data for 15 days: 6 days at 0 kWh, 1 day at 8 kWh, 2 days at 9 kWh, 2 days at 11 kWh, 2 days at 16 kWh, 2 days at 23 kWh. What is the median?

steps.description: Write all 15 values in order (6 zeros, then the rest)

sections.tip: Write out ALL individual data values (including repeats) from a frequency table before finding the median position. Don't count categories — count occurrences.

sections.title: Type 2: Mean, Median, and Distribution Shape
How Skewness Affects Mean vs. Median
sections.content:
The shape of the distribution determines the relationship between mean, median, and mode:

| Distribution | Order of measures | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric (bell curve) | mean ≈ median ≈ mode | Heights of adults |
| Right-skewed (tail to the right) | mode < median < **mean** | Income distribution |
| Left-skewed (tail to the left) | **mean** < median < mode | Test scores with many high scores |

**Rule:** the mean is **pulled toward the tail**. Outliers at the high end raise the mean above the median; outliers at the low end pull the mean below.

**The median is resistant** to extreme values — adding one outlier barely changes it.

sections.title: Example: Effect of an Outlier on Mean vs. Median
sections.problem: A class of 10 students scored: 70, 72, 74, 75, 76, 78, 80, 82, 83, 150. Which is greater: the mean or the median?

steps.description: The score of 150 is an outlier (much higher than the rest). It will pull the mean upward but barely affect the median
Median = average of 5th and 6th values (76 and 78) = 77

sections.answer: Mean (84) > Median (77). The outlier of 150 raised the mean but barely affected the median.
sections.tip: Whenever you see one very high or very low value in a data set, expect mean ≠ median. The SAT often asks which is larger — look for the outlier.

sections.title: Type 3: Finding a Missing Value Given a Condition
Example: Find the Value That Creates a Target Mean
sections.problem: A student has 5 test scores: 82, 79, 90, 85, and $x$. If the mean of all 5 scores is 85, what is $x$?

steps.description: The mean is the sum divided by count. Set the sum equal to mean × count

sections.tip: Strategy: if you need the mean to equal a target value, set the SUM equal to (target mean × number of items). Then solve for the missing item.

sections.title: Type 4: Box Plots and Quartiles
Reading a Box Plot
sections.content:
A **box plot** (box-and-whisker plot) shows five summary statistics:

$$\text{Min} \;|\; Q_1 \;|\; \text{Median} \;|\; Q_3 \;|\; \text{Max}$$

- **Box:** spans from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$
- **Line inside the box:** the **median** (Q2)
- **Whiskers:** extend to the minimum and maximum values
- **Width of the box = IQR** (interquartile range = Q3 − Q1): represents the spread of the middle 50% of data

**What you CAN read from a box plot:** median, Q1, Q3, min, max, IQR, range
**What you CANNOT read:** the mean (requires individual values)

sections.title: Example: Read Values from a Box Plot
sections.problem: A box plot for exam scores shows: Min = 55, Q1 = 68, Median = 75, Q3 = 84, Max = 98. What are the range and IQR?
sections.tip: IQR represents the spread of the middle half of the data. It's more useful than range because it ignores outliers.

sections.title: Example: Compare Two Box Plots
sections.problem: Group A: Min=20, Q1=30, Median=45, Q3=55, Max=70. Group B: Min=15, Q1=38, Median=50, Q3=60, Max=72. Which group has a larger IQR, and which has a higher median?
sections.answer: Group A has a larger IQR (more spread). Group B has a higher median.

sections.title: Type 5: Standard Deviation — What It Measures
Standard Deviation = Spread Around the Mean
sections.content:
The **standard deviation** measures how spread out the data is from the mean.

- **Large standard deviation:** data is widely spread (values far from the mean)
- **Small standard deviation:** data is clustered tightly (values close to the mean)
- **Standard deviation = 0:** all values are identical

**On the SAT, you don't compute standard deviation.** Instead, you compare two data sets and determine which has a larger or smaller standard deviation.

**How to compare:** look at how spread out the values are. If most values are close to the mean → small SD. If values are far apart → large SD.

sections.title: Example: Compare Standard Deviations
sections.problem: Set A: {10, 10, 10, 10, 10}. Set B: {5, 8, 10, 12, 15}. Set C: {1, 5, 10, 15, 19}. Order from smallest to largest standard deviation.

steps.description: Set A: all values are identical. SD = 0
Set B: values range from 5 to 15, close to mean of 10. Set C: values range from 1 to 19, further from mean

sections.answer: $\sigma_A = 0 < \sigma_B < \sigma_C$ — Set C has the largest standard deviation.
sections.tip: Don't calculate. Just ask: 'are the values more spread out or more clustered?' The more spread out, the larger the standard deviation.

sections.title: Type 6: Adding/Removing Values — How Statistics Change
Example: Effect of Adding a New Value
sections.problem: A class of 20 students has a mean score of 72. A 21st student joins with a score of 90. What is the new mean?
sections.tip: Key formula: total = mean × count. Use this to find the original sum, update it, then divide by the new count.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Median:** sort first; middle value (odd count) or average of two middle values (even count)
**Mean vs. median:** mean is pulled toward outliers/tail; median is resistant
**Right-skewed:** mode < median < mean; left-skewed: mean < median < mode
**Box plot:** shows Q1, median, Q3, min, max — NOT the mean
**IQR = Q3 − Q1:** spread of the middle 50%; resistant to outliers
**Standard deviation:** large = spread out, small = clustered — compare visually on SAT

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Forgetting to sort before finding the median
- Even count: finding one middle value instead of averaging two
- Reading mean from a box plot (impossible — box plots don't show the mean)
- Confusing range (max−min) with IQR (Q3−Q1)
- Standard deviation: confusing 'more spread' with 'higher mean' — they're unrelated

sat_tips: Always sort before finding the median — this single step prevents most median errors
For 'find x given the mean is [value]': set sum = mean × count, then solve for x
Box plots show median directly, but NEVER the mean — watch for trick questions
When comparing standard deviations: ask 'which data set is more spread out from its mean?'
IQR is the better measure of spread when outliers are present; range is distorted by extreme values
